pairs.rationale: Both introduce Jesus being led by the Spirit into the wilderness for testing by the devil. Luke additionally describes His fullness of the Spirit and return from the Jordan.

Both temptations challenge Jesus as God's Son to make bread from stone. Luke speaks of this stone; Matthew speaks of these stones.

Jesus cites the teaching that a human does not live on bread alone. Deuteronomy continues with every word proceeding through God's mouth and its manna setting; Luke's supplied answer ends after bread alone.

Both describe the devil showing the world's kingdoms and their glory in Matthew's wording. Matthew specifies a very high mountain; Luke specifies a moment of time. This test occupies a different position in the two accounts.

Both contain the devil's offer to give Jesus the displayed kingdoms. Luke additionally claims that their authority and glory were handed over to the devil and that he gives them at will; Matthew does not repeat that claim.
Both make the devil's offered gift conditional on Jesus bowing down to worship him. Luke's wording is before me; Matthew also says falling down. No truth is granted to the tempter's claims.

Jesus' answer invokes worship and exclusive service of the Lord. The supplied Deuteronomy commands fearing and serving Him, clinging to Him and swearing by His name. The formulations differ; Luke is not presented as reproducing every clause.
Both describe the temple-pinnacle challenge to God's Son to throw Himself down. Luke names Jerusalem and puts this test after the kingdom offer; Matthew says the holy city and places it earlier.
The tempter cites God's command to angels concerning the one guarded. The psalm additionally speaks of guarding in all the person's ways; Luke's supplied citation does not repeat that phrase.
Both describe angels lifting the person upon their hands so that the foot does not strike a stone. The psalm is here cited within the devil's test; citation does not endorse the proposed jump.

Jesus answers with the prohibition on putting the Lord to the test. Deuteronomy additionally recalls testing Him at Testing in its supplied wording; Luke's answer does not repeat that historical clause.

Both conclude the temptation scene with the devil leaving Jesus. Luke adds until an opportune time; Matthew adds angels arriving and ministering. Those additions are not treated as the same statement.

Both describe Jesus' return or withdrawal into Galilee after the preceding introductory scenes. Luke emphasizes the Spirit's power and spreading report; Matthew mentions hearing that John had been handed over. Neither account is made to supply the other's stated reason.

Both summarize Jesus teaching in synagogues during His Galilean activity. Luke adds universal praise; Matthew adds kingdom proclamation and healing. The added clauses are not attributed to both verses.

Both place Jesus teaching in His homeland synagogue on a Sabbath. Luke explicitly names Nazareth, His upbringing, custom and standing to read; Mark mentions His disciples and the hearers' astonishment. No merged chronology of the visits is imposed.

Luke identifies the scroll as Isaiah before the quotation in the following verses. Isaiah supplies the anointing, good news, release, sight and acceptable-year language; Luke's scroll-handling detail is not independently narrated there.

Both speak of the Lord's Spirit, anointing, good news to the poor, release to captives and sight for the blind. Isaiah also mentions healing the brokenhearted; Luke's supplied verse instead continues with releasing the oppressed.

In the context of His Isaiah reading, Jesus declares the Scripture fulfilled today. The referenced Isaiah passage supplies the anointing and mission language He has just read; the fulfillment claim is Luke's presentation of Jesus' declaration.

Both hometown scenes combine wonder at Jesus with reference to His familiar family. Luke asks whether He is Joseph's son; Mark calls Him the carpenter and Mary's son and names other relatives. The family descriptions are retained as different formulations.

Jesus' reference to Elijah being sent to the Zarephath widow corresponds to God's command that he go there, where a widow was appointed to sustain him. The place-name forms remain those of the supplied passages.

Luke recalls Naaman's cleansing in Elisha's time; Kings narrates his washing, restored flesh and return to the man of God. Kings' account supplies this cleansing, not an exhaustive claim about every leprous person in Israel.
